articles.title: “OUT OF THE EATER CAME FORTH FOOD”
articles.author: E. C. Burr

paragraphs.text: On these occasions for ministry in relation to the death of a beloved brother or sister I think that things come before us in three areas. First, of course, as always, is the promotion of the glory of Christ, the second is the comfort of the bereaved, the third is what the Lord might have for the saints. I do not say that they necessarily fall in that order, save that the glory of Christ will always have the pre-eminent place in the affections of the brethren.

If we think of this scripture in relation to the death of Christ it is familiar ground to us that “out of the eater came forth food. And out of the strong … sweetness “. I think that that is the normal portion and experience of the saints as they contemplate the death of, the Lord Jesus.

The occasion which gave rise to this riddle of Samson’s was when a young lion roared against him, and the Spirit came on him “and he rent it as one rends a kid”. It speaks to us of the glory of the Lord Jesus going into death, “who by the eternal Spirit offered himself spotless to God” (Hebrews 9: 14), and all the evidence of the death of Christ is that, going into death, He “rent it as one rends a kid”. There was a loud cry, there was an earthquake, the stone was rolled away and the guards were paralysed—the glory of the display of the Father’s operations in raising Christ from the dead. You can see that the power of the Lord Jesus going into death rent it “as one rends a kid”, and it has no more power.

Of course it has power in relation to what is natural in us, and that brings the sorrow and the grief which the breaking of the natural ties necessarily involves, but Christ going into death has broken its power, and He has come out of it.

Well may we sing, ‘His be the Victor’s name’; He has rent it “as one rends a kid”. This is why there is a disposition of hope, and even of glory, in relation to the burial of a saint; because Christ has been into death and come out of it in power. Out of the eater has come forth food. What food there is in the resurrection of Christ! We were reminded last night in London of the necessity of one being “a witness with us of his resurrection”, Acts 1: 22.
What glory there is in the food that has come out of the eater being rent. We touch the greatness of what Christ is in resurrection first and find Him as food, I suppose, as Saviour.

He would not be Saviour if He were not out of death but, as Paul affirms, He is out of death—“now Christ is raised from among the dead” (1 Corinthians 15: 20) and He is gloriously great. The first way we think of Him is as Saviour, and we feed on that—
‘Jesus! our Saviour, Shepherd, Friend,
Thou Prophet, Priest, and King’.

What glorious things these are to feed on, made available to us because He has rent the power of death “as one rends a kid”. You can add to that, Son of God, Son of Man, Son of David—the glory of everything that is His. I was thinking on Lord’s day in preaching that you could almost say that “Him who knew not sin” is a name of Christ. There is only one Person to whom that could be applied.

What food there is out of His death, and what sweetness too. Out of the strong has come forth sweetness. ‘How sweet the Name of Jesus sounds in a believer’s ear!’ How blessed it is to contemplate the Man who is out of death and to find that He is out of what naturally is bitter, and, in one sense, was bitter to Him, and that out of that has come sweetness. These things, beloved, are for our contemplation and they promote the glory of Christ in the souls of the saints.

Then there is comfort for our beloved sister. In measure we enter into this with her. We have known our beloved brother and we have loved him, loved him for his service and for his spirit, for his grace, his tenderness—many things might be said of our beloved brother. It is hardly necessary to enter into them on an occasion like this which is not for the acclamation of those who are dead, but is for the current continuance of the testimony. But we have known our brother among us. None of us has known him as our beloved sister has known him. The breaking of natural ties is the sorrowful consequence of sin coming into the world, and many of us have known the breaking of these ties. There can be no tie broken in death like that of marriage. The intimacy of the link and the loss it creates—how food is needed then! How food is needed to nourish and strengthen the soul, but the food is out of the death of Christ and out of His glory as raised from it. And even out of the sorrow there is sweetness, sweetness in the knowledge and possession of the love of the Lord Jesus Christ.

How blessed! May this be ministered, beloved brethren, to our beloved sister abundantly—food and sweetness. May these be her portion. We may say, as observing these things, that our beloved sister will need them. May she find food and sweetness.

But, beloved, what for the rest of us? Our brother prayed at the beginning that things might bear on the local assembly, and, as bearing on that, they bear on the church universally. Out of death, will there be food? Is that what the local brethren are committed to?—our beloved brother who fed them a great deal having departed to be with Christ, that there will still be food? that there might even be more food? Are the young men in the place committed to food for the saints and thus for the church that out of the eater should come forth food? Out of what would have consumed food there should come that which supplies food. Beloved, are the local brethren committed to nourishing what there is of Christ in an assembly way in this locality? That should be one result of death, that out of it comes food; otherwise the eater will consume and he will go on consuming, and unless, in that sense, he is turned round to be a supply there will be loss as a result of death.

“Out of the eater came forth food, And out of the strong ... sweetness”. Beloved, are the local brethren committed to that too—committed to there being sweetness in the local assembly position in St. Albans? Are we in London? Are the saints everywhere? Many things come up which test us as to sweetness. We remember that in Jotham’s parable the fig tree says, “Should I leave my sweetness?”, Judges 9: 11. Beloved, do we think of the local assembly as a place where sweetness is to be known? Often it is interpreted in relation to the way it could be spoken of naturally, and in that sense it cloys, just as there are other scriptures that lead us to have reservations about honey. In this scripture honey is right. In this scripture honey is the result of death. Are we going to find, beloved, that there is sweetness? Not the astringency or rigour of the law, from which all the glory of the death of Christ has delivered us, but the sweetness that knows how to dispose of and how to arrange things in relation to what has been brought to light through the glad tidings. He has “brought to light life and incorruptibility by the glad tidings”, 2 Timothy 1: 10. That is sweetness coming out of the strong. How blessed!

At the end of Luke you have it manifest. He came out of death, and where there had been bitterness and sorrow among the disciples—“We had hoped that he was the one who is about to redeem Israel” (Luke 24: 21); you can see that they are still in the bitterness of it—as He comes in there is sweetness. I am not thinking merely of the broiled fish and the honeycomb, but the sweetness that comes out of His death in the word “beginning at Jerusalem”—“that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations beginning at Jerusalem” (Luke 24: 47, 48)—that is, “Out of the strong came forth sweetness”. Instead of judgment being visited as a result of the way in which the Son of Man, the Son of God, had been treated, “repentance and remission of sins” is preached in His name beginning at the very place where He was crucified. “Out of the strong came forth sweetness”.
Well, beloved, may we find it in our localities! There is probably not a locality which could not do with more of this kind of sweetness.
‘The river of His grace,
Through righteousness supplied,
Is flowing o’er the barren place
Where Jesus died’.
Out of the strong has come forth sweetness. May we find comfort and support and means of advance in this, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: THE DEATH OF A PRIEST
articles.author: A. A. Bellamy
articles.meeting: Words at the burial of Mr, C. Middleton, St

paragraphs.text: The death of a priest, beloved brethren, is felt throughout the priestly family. The poignancy of the death of a priest is impressed upon us at this time. One had thought of Jehoiada as having great distinction in his death. Not only had he contributed effectively in his life to the support of what was for God, but he had been faithful—a faithful man, and able to instruct others also. The service of Jehoiada was rendered not only personally, but in the preservation of the royal seed his wife had a very definite part. One has not to emphasize it unduly, but we have known and observed such service in the life of our brother and his beloved wife, our sister, with us today. Jehoiada was distinguished in his death. The Spirit refers to his having “done good … toward God”. That is the true priestly feature, that God is paramount in the mind of the priest, “toward God and toward his house”. There are many here present today, and most of all his local brethren, who will know what has been done in that connection, and it remains by way of example and stimulation to us all. What has now ceased in the service of our brother is to be carried forward, and first and foremost in his own locality.

It says in Hebrews that death comes in as hindering continuity. That is the simple fact—“many priests ... being hindered from continuing by death”. Then our attention is directed to Christ, beloved brethren, away from the scene of death to the One who has the priesthood, and how much is involved in that. One would refer especially to the ministry of comfort, “For we have not a high priest not able to sympathise with our infirmities, but tempted in all things in like manner, sin apart”, Hebrews 4: 15. Everything is in His hand. God has placed everything there. Nothing will fail. We may be perfectly composed in confidence and faith in the One who has the priesthood unchangeable. He does not delegate it; He has it and He exercises it Himself. He has it intransmissible.

One thought of Paul’s departure, and the personal side. It comes into view as the public apostolic service is concluded, his departure from the midst of his brethren at Miletus. How much he had left with them! Beloved brethren, how much has been left with us, how much entrusted to us. What are we going to do with it? Is there to be a slowing down, is there to be an increase in laxity? Far rather is there to be the principle of continuity. Although death may hinder continuity in certain connections, we have part in a living order of things, in a system which has its centre in the One whose life has been taken from the earth, which involves far more than that He died here. His life has been taken from the earth, but it continues in heaven, it continues in the glorious exercise of His headship in relation to the assembly, His body, which is here upon earth.

So Paul is leaving the brethren with their sorrow—it says, “specially pained by the word which he had said, that they would no more see his face”. One just thought of what he was leaving behind and how he was entrusting things to others. He was charging these elders as to continuing their service on a certain level. What a service it is! “Take heed therefore to yourselves, and to all the flock, wherein the Holy Spirit has set you as overseers, to shepherd the assembly of God, which he has purchased with the blood of his own”, Acts 20: 28. It was no local matter, merely, but the whole range of divine interests, the assembly on earth. Our brother, if one may refer again to his service, had such an outlook. He was not in any sense confined in his prayers and exercises, as many of us can witness, he had before him the whole assembly, and the shepherding of it, down to certain details in his service which many of us can bear witness to. Well now, beloved brethren, this character of service is to be continued in the energy of the Spirit amongst us, by brothers and sisters, and in our local settings. May it be so for His name’s sake.

articles.title: FEAR NOT, FAINT NOT, FAIL NOT
articles.author: J. G. Chalmers

paragraphs.text: The Lord Jesus would speak to us tonight from His own words. We live in a day when what is material occupies a large place in the minds and lives of men, when men are getting very anxious and fearful at the trend of things publicly, but the Lord Jesus would say to our hearts now, “Be not in anxiety ... your Father knows that ye have need of these things”. Let us each challenge our hearts as to whether we have implicit confidence in our Father to see us through in regard to our temporal needs.

There are far greater things to occupy our attention—spiritual, heavenly, eternal things. The Lord Jesus says here, “Seek his kingdom”. Matthew, in his account, adds the word “first”—“Seek ye first” (Matthew 6: 33), impressing us with what is to have prime place with us.

Then, in our scripture, He says, “Fear not, little flock”. This is how the Lord regards those who are attached to Him in the midst of the world (see footnote to verse 32 in N.T.), and He would comfort and assure them. Then, “It has been the good pleasure of your Father to give you the kingdom”. The good pleasure of the Father!—wonderful! Let the glory of that come home to our souls.

We had a touch on Lord’s day as to what is revealed to babes; “Yea, Father, for thus has it been well-pleasing in thy sight”, Matthew 11: 26. “Good pleasure” and “well-pleasing”—what touches for our souls! There would be a moral link between the “babes” and the “little flock”, and the Lord Jesus would impress upon us that the Father has great delight in giving things to such. Here it is the kingdom, but other scriptures show us that He gives much more, such as “all things” (Romans 8: 32) and “every spiritual blessing”, Ephesians 1: 3. Let us then seek to apprehend increasingly by faith those things that the Father has given us in His good pleasure, and draw upon the help of the Holy Spirit to make them good in our souls.

The purport of the parable in Luke 18 is that we should always pray and not faint. We are in a very testing time, with much pressure on every hand, and if that occupies us unduly we shall get downcast, be overwhelmed, and faint. Well, beloved brethren, the Lord does not want us to faint so He exhorts us to pray always. He speaks in verse 7 of God’s elect crying to Him day and night, a most touching reference to the deep feelings of the faithful remnant of the Jews as they go through the period of unprecedented suffering, their faith being tried as they await God’s intervention. In our day things publicly will get worse and worse, the faith and courage of the saints will be severely tried, but what a resource we have in prayer!—an outlet from all that is around, a blessed inlet to the presence of God, where we can unburden our hearts and make our requests known to One who is fully sympathetic and understanding. As we do this, God fills our hearts with a sense of peace, the peace of God, and turns our thoughts to the glorious Man in His presence, the Man Christ Jesus, in whom all His thoughts are immutably secured. Thus we are strengthened inwardly—“They that wait upon Jehovah shall renew their strength”, Isaiah 40: 31. Let us then be persons characterised by prayer so that we can go onward and forward in the testimonial position in moral triumph and superiority.

Lastly, in Luke 22 we have a touching reference to the priestly service of our Lord Jesus Christ. Satan has demanded to have all the disciples; he is after the wheat, what has cost the Lord Jesus so much and is precious to Him. The Lord Jesus has every right to the wheat—Satan has none whatever—his objective is to deprive God of His pleasure in His saints and to obliterate the testimony. But he will not succeed. Indeed, the Lord in using the word “brethren” in this verse, “confirm thy brethren”, indicates to us that what is collective will go right through, and we can be assured that the service of God will be sustained assembly-wise in the power of the Holy Spirit right to the end of the dispensation. But any one of us might fail, for Satan studies each one of us to exploit the tendencies of our flesh to bring us down.

Let us then have a thorough judgment of the flesh, and have no confidence in the flesh. We would gather from the Lord Jesus praying for Peter that He intercedes for each one of us individually. What a High Priest we have, ever living to make intercession for us! His desire is that we might be inwardly strengthened by faith and be in moral power in the testimony. In praying for Peter, the Lord Jesus is a Model for us, for if we see any brother or sister growing cold in their affections and inclined to turn back, we can render them a great service in praying for them. We want all the brethren to be preserved livingly in the testimony of our Lord and in the service of God. All we have now is the rest of our time and we can, like Peter, use it rightly to confirm and comfort each other. May we each be encouraged then by these touches from Christ—fear not; faint not; fail not; for His name’s sake.

articles.title: THE GOD WITH WHOM WE HAVE TO DO
articles.author: L. A. Barlow

paragraphs.text: Just a simple touch, beloved, as I believe an occasion like this would leave with us the consciousness that we are having to do with God. We are having to do with God in a most glorious way, having to do with the God of glory, having to do with a God whose thoughts are glorious and who has purposed in the infinite wisdom and love of His own heart to bring many sons to glory. How good therefore to live in this dispensation when God is working out the greatest of His thoughts, things that are said to be becoming to Him, truly suitable to what He is in His own glorious Being. It is wonderful to think, as the glories of Christ have come before us, of the infinitude of love that has operated in such a way that not only is Christ made glorious to us, but there are going to be persons who are glorious with Him, as like Him.

What a privilege to see Jesus at the present time; indeed, the Spirit of God has helped us in these occasions to see Jesus. In spite of the conditions around, our outlook has been directed to that glorious Person and to see Him crowned with glory and honour. It is in this way that there is a sphere of things where the glories that will yet shine out publicly in the blessed Son of Man are already appreciated and understood and where there is an answer in affection to His own heart. How glorious it is to have any part in such things. It is wonderful to consider that not only is God glorious, but He has operated in the hearts of persons in view of bringing them to glory. What encouragement, and how elevating, as we are lifted up in the realisation that, through wonderful grace, we are the subjects of these operations of God.

I read that scripture in Romans because what must surely run alongside this sense of glory is the consciousness of sovereign mercy. What a need there is to be maintained in our souls in the recognition of God as God. Paul brings up this matter of a man raising a question with God and he says in effect, ‘Well, God is God’. What rights He has; what rights He has to do just what He will. What rights He has to effect everything, beloved, in the expression of Himself thus. How sobering it is to have to do with God. Both these two things should be carried in our souls all the time we are here, the blessedness of having to do with God known in grace, and yet, on the other hand, the reverential fear which rightly becomes persons who have to do with such a God. So He is seen here operating just as He will, and as perfectly justified in all that He does. Think of that—the solemnity of it! It must come home to every saved soul—Why did not God operate in a different way in relation to me? What a sense it gives our souls of the riches of His glory—“Vessels of mercy ... prepared for glory”.

May we be encouraged in the knowledge that we are having to do with God, beloved, God in relation to the greatness of His thoughts, and we on our side just vessels of mercy prepared for glory. This will enable our hearts to rise up in a note of thanksgiving to the God who would strengthen and encourage us as we are affected in simplicity and reality by any experience of His presence amongst us of a truth. May He help us to realise it increasingly.

These scriptures, dear brethren, may serve to bring out further the truth as to the supremacy of Christ. How illuminating it is to realise that the Person who has won your affections is the One who will finally assert His own supremacy in view of concluding everything for the pleasure and glory of

God. God began in christianity with the supremacy of Jesus made Lord and Christ. God will conclude things in Him. I suppose there is no book in the whole canon of Scripture which brings out the supremacy of Christ more than the book of Revelation, the wonderful way in which everything according to God is concluded with the assertion in authority and power of the supremacy of the Man in whom everything centres for God. So as His supremacy marked the beginning it is also going to mark the end.

Now what I particularly want to draw attention to in this passage in Revelation 3 is the little phrase, descriptive of the Lord Jesus, “He who opens”; not to occupy you exactly with what is opened, but to attract us freshly to the Person through whom disclosures are to come at the end of the dispensation. Whilst from one point of view the truth is all out the word of God was completed through the Lord’s servant the apostle Paul—nevertheless on our side there is need of great expansion in the experience of that truth, and it involves the consistent, current service of Christ in the way that He alone can open things up to us. So I speak of Him as “He who opens”.

Revelation 19 is majestic in the way it shows the supremacy of Christ in regard of the subjugation of every alien force. One on a white horse called Faithful and True, having a name written which no one knows. How great Christ is! Mr. Taylor spoke of that name written as involving what is inscrutable in the Person of the Lord Jesus. Remember that there is that in Christ which will always be beyond us. The greatness of who He is remains unalterable, unchanged by the passage of time; it will remain eternally—the greatness of the Person of the Lord Jesus. But then He has another name written on His garments and on His thigh, the place of strength—King of kings and Lord of lords. The very Person whom we have come to know in our experience is the One who in that day will take issue with the great enemies that will then be extant, and the beast and the false prophet will be taken first and dealt with. What irony is in that, that the commanders-in-chief of Satan’s forces will be dealt with first in that great final conflict, and what will emerge is the supremacy of Christ.

So He is supreme; that is conclusive. He has gained the mastery over every evil force. He has already done that; He has been into death. He presents Himself earlier in the book as having the keys of death and of hades (Revelation 1: 18). How assuring that is! Are you under pressure, dear brother, or sister? Do matters of adversity seem, as far as you are concerned, to be out of control? Be assured there is a Man who is supreme in regard of the forces of evil; the same One who is to be supreme in your affections, the Person of the Lord Jesus. A wonderful truth governing the dispensation is that a Man has gained mastery over Satan. So things are controlled now for the saints; we are not to be downcast or overwhelmed by the pressure; but rather sustained as in the knowledge of the One who has the keys of death and of hades. So that although Satan came with all power and force against the Lord Jesus, what is allowed to come against the saints now is controlled. God’s infinitely wise hand permits things to happen for discipline, for teaching, and instruction, in view of the results that He has in mind being reached in His people. All is now controlled by the One who is supreme.
Those two in Luke 24 were going away from the divine centre, for the moment discouraged, and together in their discouragement. Do not let us get together on those lines, dear brethren.

It is good to be together in what is positive, but let us not get together on lines of discouragement. They were moving further and further away. We have referred to some who have diverted; they are still our brethren. We still have obligations in relation to them and should still have intense interest in them. What comes out in this passage is the Lord’s deep interest in two persons who for the moment were not on the main line. How far He was prepared to go! Of course, He can go where we cannot go, but I believe we learn through this incident the value the Lord places on His own work, even in persons who for the moment may be wayward. “He made as though he would go farther”, but “they constrained him”. That is very interesting; two persons for the moment not in Jerusalem, off-centre we may say, and yet the Lord is constrained by these persons. See the value He placed upon them, the way He was prepared, for the moment, to tarry with them in view of their being gained. I believe this is the way that what is of God in persons will be revived, as freshly they come to it in the experience of their souls that Jesus is supreme. He drew near to them and “interpreted to them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself”. Later on they say, “He opened the scriptures to us”, and later, as to the company, “He opened their understanding to understand the scriptures” (Luke 24: 45). Oh that we might get that kind of understanding of the Scriptures! What sort of understanding have we of the word of God?

How dependent we need to be as to its use. Mr. Darby stressed that we need to keep the word and the Spirit together (Coll. Wrtgs. (N.S. Vol. 4, p.63). We need, too, the touch of Christ in view of the Scriptures becoming the word of God to us.

So the Lord gives them a touch from Himself. Oh that we may yet see persons who are within range of us, dear brethren, get a touch that will bring them back. I think we should be very thankful for those who are within range, recoverable, those who have not committed themselves to the great current of apostasy that is running in the world or to what is out of keeping with the name of Christ religiously. Such persons may yet respond with an alacrity that may surprise us to a touch from Christ. The Lord took the house-father’s place and made Himself known to them. Then they retrace their steps to Jerusalem, coming back into the area where His headship would be the normal experience. You see, He did not stay with them in that far-away place. It may be that you need to make a move; it may be that you need to take a journey spiritually to get back into the area where the headship of Christ is a normal and known experience. The way I think it will be reached is by a fresh assertion in your own soul of the supremacy of Him who is prepared to open things up to you.

In 1 Kings 10 we have typically a person who is prepared to make a journey to reach Christ. It is important that we get a view of Christ, not simply on His own, but as the centre of the divine system. Solomon had a wonderful order of things under his hand. Had he travelled to where the queen of Sheba was she might have apprehended his wisdom, she might have got the answers to her questions, but it would not have had the same effect on her as the view she had of the system of things of which Christ, in type, was the centre. So she undertakes this journey and comes to prove Solomon with enigmas, hard questions. Has anyone here got an enigma—something that is perplexing you? You find that there is not really an obvious answer to it, and perhaps you have conversed with this one and that one—for we tend first to look to men for the answer, perhaps to those who may be near to us, or to those whom we think would give us the sort of answer we would prefer to hear. How ready the flesh is to exploit any situation! As a circumstance confronts you which is perplexing, take it to Christ. The Lord is available for the explanation of hard questions. The queen of Sheba came with all this wealth, and with her problems, into the presence of Solomon, type of Christ in His position of unchallenged supremacy, and available in view of the opening up of the answers to questions which none other could solve.

I believe it to be a point of experience, valuable beyond anything else, when we find that there is only one Person to whom we can turn, and that is Christ. We are thankful for the brethren; we would not be without them; to look round upon them today is to see the evidence of what God has done, and we thank Him for it; but we need to come to the point, as helped of the Spirit, where our only resource is Christ; this will have a marked effect on our outlook. The queen of Sheba is affected not only by Solomon but by the greatness of the system over which he presides. She saw his wisdom, the house that he had built, the food of his table, the deportment of his servants, the order of service of his attendants and their apparel, his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up to the house of Jehovah, and there was no more spirit in her.

This will deliver us from the appeal of every other system. The Spirit would give us a glimpse of God’s world. Man’s world is offering its attractions; how tempting, and not only for young persons (let us not lay the burdens too heavily upon them); it is making its bid for those who are older too. Persons who are secure are persons who have an apprehension of a realm where Christ’s supremacy is unchallenged and where there is no problem too hard to solve. The realm of the assembly is thus a place where questions can be answered. Why then do exercises drag on? Why is it that matters become extended? Is it, perhaps, that the needed state of subjection is lacking so that when the answer comes we are slow to submit ourselves to it? The power of Christ is just as great today as it will be in the day to come. His greatness remains as it was at the beginning, as it will be at the end; but the wonder of it is that the experience of it is available even now to persons who come into the assembly in a spirit of subjection.

So the Lord addresses Himself in Revelation 3, as we have been taught, to a wonderful condition of things developed under the hand of the Spirit. Philadelphia represents a place where the Lord is loved. Thank God for the revival amongst us of assembly affection for Christ. He says, “Thou hast a little power ... and hast not denied my name”, and “hast kept the word of my patience”. The Lord was affected by what existed in the church at Philadelphia.

We must be careful not to claim things, dear brethren, but let us be concerned to provide something that affects the Lord. The way He presents Himself indicates the pleasure He finds in what is for Him in Philadelphia. In spite of all the departure—think of the dislocation that the addresses to the other churches bring into view, think of the inroads of Satan—what comes out here is that the Lord is supreme and stands directly in relation to a state of things that is pleasing to Him.

Whatever comes in publicly cannot alter this fact that the Lord is supreme. That supremacy is to be proved in its detail, dear brethren, in a sphere that is suited to Him. So He says, ‘These things saith the holy, the true; He that has the key of David, He who opens, and no one shall shut’. The key of David is a wonderful suggestion. He is able to open up precious positive truth to us in this wonderful realm where what is for God’s pleasure is in view. The Lord would present Himself to us as having the key of David still! He is prepared to open things in a fresh and a vital sense to us. How thankful we are for what has gone before. You will remember that Isaac in Genesis 26 dug again the wells that his father had dug. Let us make sure that those wells are all dug. Let us make sure that the ministries on our bookshelves are valued and that the earth is removed and the water supply is flowing through the wells that our fathers have dug. Then as he proceeds Isaac digs other wells and he finds that there is additional experience, what is fresh.

I believe we are in the time when we should be enlarged as to what may be additional in the spiritual realm. Our testimony is not simply to be repetitive. We are to retain all that has gone before, particularly the principles that have been stood for, principles that have been fought for, battles that have been fought and won. We are to carry all that forward; but there is also to be what is fresh. We are not simply going over old ground in that sense, but we are in the presence of what is divinely fresh and living. The word is Rehoboth—“Jehovah has made room for us”, Genesis 26: 22. What is the secret of this? It is the supremacy of Christ as “He who opens”, the One who does it, the One through whom the revelation of God has come. How much has come through Jesus, and He is the One who will open up things freshly to us in the divine realm.

So this section is like the divine investiture of the saints. The Lord says, “He that overcomes ... I will write upon him”. Think of that kind of material that He writes on. The first material God wrote on was tables of stone—hard, permanent no doubt, but hard and unresponsive. What God is writing on now is sensitive and responsive to Himself. “I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven, from my God, and my new name”. What is personal to Christ is prominent. It shows a capacity in the saints which is wonderful, that they are able to receive what belongs to Christ. It shows close correspondence between Him and them that they can receive those impressions, not in a passing or transient sense, but as written upon them. Let us then be impressionable in the assembly. As we follow up what He brings in we find that the divine writing is proceeding under the hand of the One who is able to make such wonderful disclosures to us. May we see that the One who will yet conclude everything for God is prepared to serve us thus even in these last days. May He help us, for His name’s sake.
Who first to me revealed
That I in darkness lay;
A sinner unconcealed
To God’s all-searching ray?
Thou, Holy Spirit. Thou wast He
Who sin’s conviction brought to me.
Who then to me didst show
The Saviour’s wounded side;
That I His love could know,
And in Himself could hide?
Blest Holy Spirit, Thou it wast
That told salvation to the lost.
Who bade me look above;
From self to Christ to flee?
Who told that mercy, love
Were in God’s heart for me?
O, blessed Holy Spirit, Thou
Dost witness to forgiveness now.
Who came to shed within
God’s boundless love to me?
Who keeps me free from sin
Till Jesus’ face I see?
Thou, blessed Holy Spirit, art
The One who fills with joy my heart.
Who teaches me to pray,
And guides my steps aright?
Who leads me in His way
All through earth’s dreary night?
Most Holy Spirit, Thou wast giv’n
Our Comforter and Guide to heav’n.
Who us shall never leave
When time’s for ever past?
Who shall full praise receive
When Jesus comes at last?
O Holy Spirit, with the Son
And Father Thou art ever One!

GIFTS FOR GOD It should be among our most treasured privileges that we can bring gifts to God. The priests of old brought daily offerings (literally, ‘gifts’) to Jehovah. They offered the morning and the evening lamb, and each morning and evening they brought fine flour as a continual oblation (Leviticus 6: 20). Let us take up this holy privilege. God would have each of our days set in this rich enclosure—starting and ending with our offering to Him some touch of our fresh appreciation of Christ. Let us rise to this! It is not a prolonged, formal thing. Some thought of Christ from the Scriptures becomes food for you. You enjoy it. Well, carry it a stage further—bring to God in simple thankfulness just what you have enjoyed. He will enjoy it too; it is a priestly gift. He delights in the affectionate presentation to Him of some impression of Christ by those who, by the Holy Spirit, share His love for that Man.

Then night comes. Some further touch as to the perfection of Christ has come to you during the day, and your day ends, as it began, as you simply bring to God some newly-found impression of His beloved Son. Thus are the days of the believer to be sanctified and fruitful.
